title: A seasonal network of caravans and ships converging on one city, never twice by the same road
register: documentary, and skeptical of the chroniclers' round numbers
summary: No caliph, sultan, or shipping company ever owned the road to Mecca; it was reassembled every year out of a caliph's water engineers, a provincial governor's escort, a sharif's customs post, a tribe's wells, and a merchant's camels, timed by a lunar calendar that refused to sit still in any one season. What moved on it was pilgrims, but also bullion, textiles, scholarship, slaves, and disease, and what ended it was not one conquest but a slow layering of steamships, quarantine stations, a railway, and a new Arabian state on top of a system that had already survived Qarmatian sackings and a annihilated caravan in 1757.

nodes.name: Mecca
nodes.note: The compulsory ritual center and principal final market, reliant on imported grain, holding the Sacred Mosque, Zamzam, and the court of the sharif. Complaints about exactions here recur across centuries of travel accounts.

nodes.name: Medina
nodes.note: Not a constitutive rite of Hajj but incorporated by most pilgrims: a major redistribution node where the Syrian and Iraqi routes converged and Egyptian coastal routes could join the Mecca axis.

nodes.name: Mina
nodes.note: A high-load seasonal encampment for animal sacrifice and the stoning rites, chronically dependent on the same water engineering that served Arafat and Mecca.

nodes.name: Arafat
nodes.note: The standing on 9 Dhu al-Hijja without which the Hajj is invalid; a seasonal high-load node whose water provision was a chronic engineering problem addressed by Ayn Zubayda and later repairs.

nodes.name: Jeddah
nodes.note: Mecca's principal seaport, connecting Red Sea shipping to a roughly 70-80 kilometer overland leg. Fortified across Mamluk, sharifal and Ottoman phases against the Portuguese threat that reached the Red Sea in 1541 without taking the port.

nodes.name: Baghdad
nodes.note: Gathered pilgrims from Iraq, Iran and lands farther east; the caliphal center whose elite patronage, including Zubayda's, built up the Kufa-Mecca trunk.

nodes.name: Kufa
nodes.note: The traditional desert-road head; the formal Darb Zubayda is best understood as the Kufa-Mecca trunk rather than every feeder line reaching Baghdad.

nodes.name: Fayd
nodes.note: An inhabited, fortified, provisioned midpoint east of the Jabal Shammar region: depot, market, repair point, and place where travelers changed arrangements. Archaeology has revealed wells, channels, pools, mosques and fortified architecture.

nodes.name: al-Rabadha
nodes.note: A substantial early-Islamic-period station with water installations and settlement remains on the Iraqi trunk; no secure date for its decline is given in the surviving evidence.

nodes.name: Dhat 'Irq
nodes.note: Both a road station and a miqat, the legally defined place where pilgrims approaching from Iraq entered the consecrated state.

nodes.name: Basra
nodes.note: Head of a route through northeastern and central Arabia serving pilgrims from lower Iraq, Khuzistan, the Persian Gulf and sometimes Iran; often presented as a perfect parallel to the Kufa road, which overstates the uniformity of the evidence.

nodes.name: Damascus
nodes.note: Principal assembly city for the Syrian caravan and, under Ottoman rule, for pilgrims from Anatolia, the Balkans, the Caucasus, Central Asia, northern Iraq and Iran. By the eighteenth century its governor regularly also served as amir al-hajj.

nodes.name: Muzayrib
nodes.note: A major mustering and supply point where grain and equipment were accumulated before the desert crossing.

nodes.name: Ma'an
nodes.note: A long-lived market and oasis whose inhabitants provisioned caravans, with installations built or repaired by successive rulers.

nodes.name: Tabuk
nodes.note: An oasis, fort and market whose water was indispensable to the Syrian trunk, and the general area of the disastrous 1757 attack on the returning caravan.

nodes.name: al-Hijr
nodes.note: With al-'Ula, controlled a chain of northern Hijazi water and settlement sites on the road toward Medina.

nodes.name: Cairo
nodes.note: Caravan head, financial center, textile-production center and clearing point for pilgrims from the Maghrib, West Africa, the Nile valley and the Mediterranean, and home of the mahmal procession.

nodes.name: Nakhl
nodes.note: A fortress with wells, cisterns and administrative installations approximately midway across Sinai, demonstrating state investment in the pre-steam pilgrimage road.

nodes.name: Aqaba
nodes.note: A chokepoint and junction, Ayla, where Egyptian coastal and Syrian groupings could meet; Ibn Hawqal described the Egyptian coastal road in stages through here.

nodes.name: Aydhab
nodes.note: The main port for the Eastern Desert alternative to the Sinai land route, crossed by Ibn Jubayr in the twelfth century; his account emphasizes discomfort and the shipowners' limited concern for passenger safety.

nodes.name: Zabid
nodes.note: A center on the Tihama coastal plain approached by Yemeni pilgrims traveling toward Mecca, alongside Ta'izz, Sanaa, Sa'da and Najran depending on origin and political circumstance.

nodes.name: Aden
nodes.note: A port linking Indian Ocean pilgrims to western Arabia, alongside Mocha, Hudayda and al-Luhayya, and a transshipment point for ocean-going pilgrim vessels dependent on monsoon timing.

nodes.name: Surat
nodes.note: Principal Indian embarkation port for the Hajj, depicted with its pilgrim ships in the illustrated Anis al-Hujjaj guide produced in Gujarat around 1677-80.

nodes.name: Timbuktu
nodes.note: Entered the pilgrimage network's historical visibility through Mansa Musa's 1324-25 journey and remained a hub for the trans-Saharan feeder routes carrying West African pilgrims, gold, books and diplomatic gifts toward Cairo.

nodes.name: Diriyya
nodes.note: Capital of the first Saudi state, from which Saudi-Wahhabi forces seized Mecca on 30 April 1803, disrupting Ottoman-supervised arrangements before Muhammad Ali's Egyptian-Ottoman forces destroyed Diriyya itself in 1818.

nodes.name: Zubayda bint Ja'far
nodes.note: Wife of Harun al-Rashid and the network's most famous individual patron, credited with wells, pools and works on the Iraqi road and with the Meccan water system. Which surviving works she personally commissioned, and their exact expenditure, remains unresolved; the saying that she ordered spending without limit is a literary motif, not a cost record.

nodes.name: Baybars
nodes.note: The Mamluk sultan traditionally associated with instituting Cairo's mahmal procession, though the exact first year and antecedents are disputed.

nodes.name: The Sharifate of Mecca
nodes.note: Indispensable intermediaries under changing relationships with Abbasid, Fatimid, Ayyubid, Rasulid, Mamluk and Ottoman powers: they controlled local armed force, appointments, access, taxation and relations with surrounding tribes, and were needed by every outside power that claimed custodianship of the pilgrimage.

nodes.name: The Ottoman Damascus caravan command
nodes.note: By the eighteenth century the Damascus governorship and the office of amir al-hajj were regularly combined, concentrating provincial, military, fiscal and ceremonial authority in one office exposed to removal, confiscation, or execution after disaster.

nodes.name: Mansa Musa
nodes.note: His pilgrimage, conspicuous gold distribution and impact on Cairene observers are documented through Arabic sources including al-'Umari; the entourage figures commonly attached to him, often 60,000 persons and 12,000 enslaved attendants, are medieval reported figures, not independently verified counts, and his exact route beyond Cairo is not fully recoverable.

nodes.name: Ibn Jubayr
nodes.note: His journey from al-Andalus through Alexandria, Cairo, the Nile, Aydhab, a Red Sea crossing, Jeddah, Mecca, and back by the Iraqi caravan is the most useful medieval end-to-end case because it crosses maritime and overland subsystems, negotiated separately rather than bought as a through-ticket.

nodes.name: Evliya Çelebi
nodes.note: Traveled through Anatolia and Syria, joined the Damascus caravan, visited Medina and Mecca, and returned with the Egyptian caravan to Cairo, demonstrating interoperability between the two outward and return systems. His route and institutional observations are more secure than his numerical totals.

nodes.name: Husayn Pasha ibn Makki
nodes.note: Commander of the Syrian caravan held responsible and executed after the 1757 disaster near the northern Hijaz, when a coalition led principally by Bani Sakhr elements attacked the returning caravan, weakened by disputes over payments and command. Casualty totals cannot be established, but the scandal caused real political retaliation and reorganization.

nodes.name: The Darb Zubayda water system
nodes.note: Wells, masonry cisterns, dams, and channels along the Kufa road and around the ritual circuit, known collectively as Ayn Zubayda where it fed Arafat, Muzdalifa, Mina and Mecca. A durable medieval attribution to Zubayda, but not all surviving installations can be assigned to her personally; sections survived into the twentieth century before modern pumping made the historical system nonfunctional.

nodes.name: The imperial surre
nodes.note: Cash and gifts sent annually from Istanbul through Anatolia to Damascus and on to Mecca and Medina, managed by a specialized bureaucracy of treasury officials, scribes, escorts and local distributors. Surviving surre registers, recording named beneficiaries and amounts, are among the strongest quantitative sources for imperial patronage of the pilgrimage.

nodes.name: The mahmal
nodes.note: An ornate ceremonial palanquin borne on a camel, a portable symbol of sovereign patronage traditionally linked to Baybars; not to be confused with the kiswah, the Ka'ba's textile covering. Whether it carried a Qur'an varied in representation and possibly in practice.
